previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Meléndez, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of heavy alcohol use, was admitted with severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hematemesis, and chest pain after consuming two pints of vodka. His symptoms were attributed to alcoholic gastritis with hemorrhage and alcohol withdrawal, with no evidence of acute abdominal pathology on CT or ultrasound. He was managed with high-dose omeprazole, a lidocaine patch for pain, and Zofran for nausea, which resolved during the stay. He received enoxaparin for anticoagulation, started on metoprolol for heart rate control, and was treated with Bactrim for a right axillary skin infection. He remained stable, abstinent from alcohol during admission, and was discharged home with medication adjustments, follow-up plans, and counseling on alcohol cessation.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo man w/ a hx of dilated cardiomyopathy (EF 25% w/ ICD), 
afib/aflutter, and hx PE presents with chest pain and vomiting 
also incidentally found to be EtOH intoxicated.  

#EtOH INTOXICATION: Patient's blood alcohol level was 323 on 
admission, unable to provide meaningful history of past 
withdrawal but does endorse that his last drink was the 
afternoon before admission. He was placed on a CIWA scale, given 
IV thiamine, and multivitamin.  He scored > 10 on CIWA three 
times and received PO diazepam.  He received IV ativan twice 
when unable to tolerate PO.  No altered mental status or 
seizures.
.  
#NAUSEA/ VOMITING/ ABDOMINAL PAIN: Patient had non-bloody, 
non-bilious vomiting, usually after eating.  GI was contacted by 
the ED and recommended BID PPI and detox from alcohol. Has a 
AST:ALT ratio of 2:1 lending further evidence to the case that 
this patient recently consumed a large volume of alcohol and now 
has alcohol induced liver injury causing abdominal pain/nausea.  
Of note, on review of prior discharge summaries, patient has 
been found to be placing soup into his emesis basin.  Nausea was 
managed with ondansetron and compazine.  

#CHEST PAIN: Clear history of trauma as patient reports history 
of being punched in the chest. No evidence of bruising on exam 
nor evidence of rib or sternal fracture on chest imaging. 
Electrophysiology has interrogated the device which is without 
recent discharges.  Ruled out for ACS with no acute EKG changes 
and two sets of negative cardiac enzymes.  
.  
#ISCHEMIC CARDIOMYOPATHY: Depressed EF in the 20% range after 
massive MI several years ago now s/p AICD placement. 
Interrogated by EP without evidence of reccent pacer activity. 
No evidence of acute decompensation the patient's heart failure 
on exam or history.  Continued losartan, simvastatin, 
metoprolol, aspirin.

hemolysis labs negative.  Likely ___ syndrome / impaired 
conjugation, consistent with prior labs.

fall 2 weeks prior to admission with headstrike.  Normal head CT

rate control with metoprolol.  CHADS2 score is 2.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,
It was a pleasure caring for you during your recent 
hospitalization for chest pain.  The chest pain was related to 
being punched in the chest near your defibrillator.  
Cardiologists looked at your device and found that it did not 
fire.  You did not have a heart attack.

You were found to have high alcohol levels in the blood.  We 
gave you medications and monitored you to make sure you did not 
have complications of withdrawal.

Because you have an abnormal heart rhythm called atrial 
fibrillation, you should continue taking dabigatran twice daily 
to reduce the risk of stroke.  

Your nausea, vomiting, and dizziness are probably related to 
alcohol withdrawal.  There were no abnormalities in your stomach 
or intestines to cause this.

Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.
